title: CERN Starts Taking Apart the World's Biggest Atom Smasher
summary:
Under the border between France and Switzerland, there's a ring 27 kilometers around — that's longer than a marathon. It's called the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), and it's the most powerful atom smasher on Earth. Right now, workers are starting to take parts of it apart.

Here's how it works. The LHC uses thousands of magnets to steer and focus tiny particle beams. Some of the most important are called inner triplets — groups of three magnets that squeeze the beams as tightly as possible right before particles collide. The tighter the squeeze, the more collisions happen.

More collisions mean more data for scientists to study. So CERN, the lab that runs the LHC, is replacing the old inner triplets with much stronger ones. On September 7, crews cut the first magnet connection, officially starting the swap.

The new magnets use a different material — niobium-tin instead of niobium-titanium — and can create magnetic fields about 40% stronger. In total, 28 superconducting magnets will be removed and replaced. The first new quadrupole magnet should arrive in the tunnel at the start of 2029.

The old magnets have been in the LHC since it was built, installed between 2005 and 2007. After nearly 20 years, they're making way for a new generation. "It's truly remarkable to witness such a handover from one generation of innovation to the next," said Markus Zerlauth, the HiLumi LHC project leader.
why_it_matters: Big machines like the LHC are how scientists find out what the universe is made of, and the work going on now could lead to discoveries many years from now.

background_read: CERN (a big science laboratory on the border of France and Switzerland) runs the LHC with help from many countries.
The LHC is a giant ring-shaped tunnel deep underground. It speeds up tiny particles and crashes them together so scientists can learn what matter is made of.
In 2012, scientists using the LHC announced they had found the Higgs boson, a particle that helps explain why things have mass.

WHERE: In the 27-kilometer LHC ring under the border between France and Switzerland

perspectives.description: They are excited because stronger magnets mean more collisions, which means more chances to discover something new about tiny particles.

perspectives.perspective: People who worry about the cost
perspectives.description: Big upgrades take many years and a lot of money, and some wonder whether that money could help with other needs too.
They see the magnet swap as a handover from one generation of technology to the next, done carefully deep inside a tunnel.
